Chapter 9. Self-Awareness and the Path to Better Judgment.
You know, just noticing our mind’s biases and blind spots is only the beginning. The real challenge? It’s weaving that awareness into our everyday choices.
That’s where self-reflection and a bit of deliberate practice come in. They help us tap into our slower, more careful thinking—especially when it really matters.
One of the best ways to do this is by working on our metacognition. That’s just a fancy word for thinking about our own thinking. It means hitting pause, questioning those gut reactions, and looking for other possibilities.
Try asking yourself simple questions, like, “What else could this mean?” or “How might I be wrong here?” These little habits can slow down that rush to judgment and open up new perspectives.
So, what are some habits that boost self-awareness?
First, pause before making big decisions. Give yourself a moment to really think things through.
Next, go out of your way to look for evidence that disagrees with your first impression. And don’t forget to reflect on past mistakes—think about what led to them, and what you might do differently next time.
There’s another powerful tool: checklists and structured decision-making. When you break a complex choice into smaller steps, it’s much easier to spot important details that might otherwise slip by.
Just look at pilots or surgeons. They use checklists all the time to make sure nothing critical gets missed. It’s a simple habit, but it can dramatically cut down on errors.
Mindfulness is another practice worth trying. By training your attention, you get better at noticing your own thought patterns and emotional reactions.
This way, you’ll catch yourself when you’re about to jump to conclusions—giving that slower, wiser part of your mind a chance to step in.
Here are a few practical techniques you might find useful:
Use checklists when making big or complicated decisions.
Practice mindfulness to become more aware of your thoughts and feelings.
And make it a habit to regularly set aside time for reflection and review.
Building self-awareness isn’t a one-and-done kind of thing. It takes humility, a bit of curiosity, and a willingness to learn from your own experience.
But if you stick with it—even just making small, steady changes—you’ll find your judgment gets sharper and your choices become wiser over time.
